lp-simplex.title: Linear programming and the simplex method

questions.q: Where does the optimal value of $\max c^\top x$ s.t. $Ax\le b$, $x\ge 0$ live, when it is finite?
choices: At the strict interior of the feasible polyhedron
At a vertex (basic feasible solution) of the polyhedron
At the centroid of the polyhedron
Always at the origin $x=0$
questions.hint: A linear objective restricted to a bounded face is itself linear, so its maximum is attained on the boundary.
questions.explain: The fundamental theorem of LP: a linear objective over a bounded polyhedron attains its maximum at a vertex. Even on an unbounded polyhedron, when the optimum is finite, some basic feasible solution achieves it.

questions.q: Consider $\max\ 3x_1 + 2x_2$ s.t. $x_1 + x_2 \le 4$, $x_1 \le 3$, $x_1,x_2 \ge 0$. What is the optimal value?
questions.hint: Enumerate the vertices of the feasible polygon — they are $(0,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(3,1)$, $(0,4)$.
questions.explain: The four vertices are $(0,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(3,1)$, $(0,4)$, with objective values $0, 9, 11, 8$. The optimum is $11$ at $(3,1)$.

questions.q: Which statements about the simplex method are correct?
choices: Each pivot moves to an adjacent vertex with strictly improving objective (modulo degeneracy)
Simplex has worst-case polynomial pivot count on every input
Simplex runs empirically fast despite worst-case exponential behavior (Klee–Minty)
The interior-point method is a competitor that gives the first proven polynomial-time LP algorithm (Khachiyan / Karmarkar)
questions.hint: Klee–Minty exhibits a perturbed cube on which simplex visits $2^n$ vertices; that rules out one of the options.
questions.explain: Simplex pivots between adjacent BFS along improving directions; Klee–Minty cubes force $2^n$ pivots in the worst case. Smoothed analysis (Spielman–Teng) explains the empirical polynomial behavior. Khachiyan's ellipsoid method (1979) gave the first polynomial-time LP algorithm.

questions.q: If $x$ is primal-feasible for $\max c^\top x$ s.t. $Ax\le b$, $x\ge 0$, and $y$ is dual-feasible for $\min b^\top y$ s.t. $A^\top y\ge c$, $y\ge 0$, which inequality always holds?
choices: $c^\top x \ge b^\top y$
$c^\top x \le b^\top y$
$c^\top x = b^\top y$ (always)
$c^\top x + b^\top y \le 0$
questions.hint: Use $Ax\le b$ and $A^\top y\ge c$ to sandwich $y^\top A x$ from both sides.
questions.explain: Weak duality: $c^\top x \le (A^\top y)^\top x = y^\top Ax \le y^\top b = b^\top y$. Equality holds at primal–dual optima (strong duality).

questions.q: Match each combinatorial min–max theorem to its primal optimization problem.
right: max bipartite matching = min vertex cover
max edge-disjoint $s$–$t$ paths = min edge separator
max row payoff = min column payoff in zero-sum game
questions.hint: Each theorem is LP duality for a different combinatorial polytope; the primal counts the objects, the dual counts the blockers.
questions.explain: Each theorem is LP duality applied to a 0/1 LP whose constraint matrix is TU (or has integrality gap zero by structure).

questions.q: Find the error in the following student reasoning: "By weak duality, if I find any primal-feasible $x$ with $c^\top x = 7$ and any dual-feasible $y$ with $b^\top y = 5$, the LP has optimum $7$."
steps: Let $x$ be a primal-feasible point with $c^\top x = 7$.
Let $y$ be a dual-feasible point with $b^\top y = 5$.
By weak duality, $c^\top x \le b^\top y$, so $7 \le 5$ — both points are consistent.
Conclude: the LP optimum is $c^\top x = 7$.
questions.hint: Recall the inequality direction from weak duality.
questions.explain: Step 2 is the error: weak duality demands $c^\top x \le b^\top y$ for every feasible pair. If $7 > 5$, then $x$ or $y$ is in fact NOT feasible — the student's two feasibility claims are mutually inconsistent. There is no valid LP for which both can hold.

questions.q: On a directed network $(G, s, t, c)$, after running max-flow to optimality, the reachable set from $s$ in the residual graph $G_f$ is $S$. Why is $(S, V\setminus S)$ a minimum cut?
choices: By construction — every edge from $S$ to $V\setminus S$ has $f(e) = c(e)$, so cut capacity equals flow value, and weak duality gives the min cut
Because $t \in S$ at optimum
Because $|S|$ is minimised among all cuts
Because every edge from $V\setminus S$ to $S$ has $f(e) = 0$ only
questions.hint: Every cut bounds every flow; equality means both are optimal.
questions.explain: At optimality, no augmenting path exists, so every forward edge from $S$ to $V\setminus S$ is saturated ($f(e)=c(e)$) and every backward edge has $f(e)=0$. The net flow across the cut equals the cut capacity, which also equals $|f|$. Since every cut $\ge$ every flow, both are simultaneously optimal.

questions.q: On a network where every edge has unit capacity, the max-flow / min-cut value equals the number of edge-disjoint $s$–$t$ paths (Menger). For the complete bipartite graph $K_{3,3}$ oriented left-to-right with $s$ as a super-source above the left side and $t$ as a super-sink below the right side, how many edge-disjoint $s$–$t$ paths are there?
questions.hint: The bottleneck is the source-side $s\to L$ or sink-side $R\to t$ — both have 3 unit-capacity edges.
questions.explain: The min cut is the 3 edges from $s$ to $L$ (or 3 from $R$ to $t$). Hence max-flow = 3 and there are 3 edge-disjoint $s$–$t$ paths.

questions.q: Place the steps of the Edmonds–Karp max-flow algorithm in order.
items: BFS from $s$ in $G_f$ to find a shortest augmenting path to $t$
Push the bottleneck capacity of the path through $f$
Repeat until no augmenting path exists; the current $f$ is optimal
questions.hint: Each iteration rebuilds the residual graph, BFS for a new path, augments by the bottleneck.
questions.explain: Edmonds–Karp: initialise with zero flow; iteratively (residual graph → BFS shortest path → augment by bottleneck) until BFS finds no $s$–$t$ path. The $O(|V||E|^2)$ bound comes from BFS-derived monotone shortest distances.

questions.q: Berge's lemma characterises maximum matchings as exactly the matchings $M$ such that:
choices: No vertex has more than one matching edge
There is no $M$-augmenting path (an alternating path between two unmatched vertices)
Every vertex is matched
$M$ contains a perfect matching
questions.hint: Augmenting paths flip non-matching to matching and vice versa along the path, gaining one matched edge.
questions.explain: Berge: $M$ is maximum iff no augmenting path exists. If a path $v_0 \to v_1 \to \cdots \to v_{2k+1}$ alternates non-matching/matching/non-matching and starts and ends unmatched, flipping yields $|M|+1$ matched edges.

questions.q: By König–Egerváry, in the bipartite graph with $L=\{a,b,c\}$, $R=\{1,2,3\}$ and edges $\{(a,1),(a,2),(b,2),(c,2),(c,3)\}$, what is the size of a maximum matching?
questions.hint: Try to match each left vertex; with 5 edges and only 3 right vertices, the bottleneck is on the right.
questions.explain: A maximum matching is $\{(a,1),(b,2),(c,3)\}$, size 3. The minimum vertex cover is also size 3 (e.g. $\{1,2,3\}$), confirming König's theorem.

questions.q: Which statements about maximum matching in general (non-bipartite) graphs are correct?
choices: Edmonds' blossom algorithm runs in polynomial time
Berge's lemma still characterises maximum matchings by absence of augmenting paths
König–Egerváry generalises directly to non-bipartite graphs
Odd cycles (blossoms) require special handling; naive bipartite-style search fails
questions.hint: König holds in bipartite graphs only — try the triangle for a counterexample.
questions.explain: Edmonds (1965) gave the polynomial algorithm via blossom contraction. Berge's lemma is graph-agnostic. König–Egerváry fails on the triangle: max matching = 1, min vertex cover = 2.

questions.q: Why does total unimodularity of $A$ guarantee that LP optima of $\max c^\top x$ s.t. $Ax\le b$, $x\ge 0$ are integer for integer $b$?
choices: Because Cramer's rule expresses BFS coordinates as ratios of subdeterminants of $A$, and TU forces those denominators to be $\pm 1$
Because TU matrices are square
Because integer programs always have integer optima
Because the simplex method only uses integer arithmetic
questions.hint: BFS coordinates are $x_B = B^{-1} b$ where $B$ is a basis submatrix; by Cramer, each is a subdeterminant ratio.
questions.explain: Hoffman–Kruskal: at each BFS, basic variables are $x_B = B^{-1} b$; Cramer's rule writes each entry as a ratio with $\det B$ in the denominator. TU forces $\det B \in \{-1,0,+1\}$, so the BFS is integer.

questions.q: Which of the following matrices are totally unimodular?
choices: Vertex–edge incidence matrix of a bipartite graph
Signed (head $=-1$, tail $=+1$) incidence matrix of a directed graph
Vertex–edge incidence matrix of $C_3$ (the triangle)
Matrix with consecutive-ones property (each row has a contiguous block of 1s)
questions.hint: Odd cycles break bipartite TU; one of the four listed is an odd cycle.
questions.explain: Bipartite incidence, directed signed incidence, and consecutive-ones matrices are all TU. The triangle is the standard counterexample: its incidence matrix has $\det = \pm 2$.

questions.q: Find the error in the following argument: "My ILP's constraint matrix $A$ has $\det A = 1$, so $A$ is totally unimodular, so the LP relaxation has integer vertices and solves the ILP."
steps: $A$ is the constraint matrix; compute $\det A = 1$.
By Hoffman–Kruskal, every BFS of $\{x\ge 0 : Ax\le b\}$ is integer.
Conclude: the LP relaxation has integer optimum and solves the ILP.
questions.hint: TU is a property of every square submatrix, not just $A$ itself.
questions.explain: Step 1 is correct, and steps 2–4 follow only if 'TU' is correctly applied. Step 2 is the error: TU requires every square submatrix (every $k\times k$ minor for every $k$) to have determinant in $\{-1,0,+1\}$, not just $A$ as a whole. A matrix with $\det A = 1$ can have, say, a $2\times 2$ subminor of $2$ — the bipartite incidence of $C_3$ is one such example.

questions.q: Edmonds' matching polytope theorem describes $P_{\mathrm{match}}(G)$ for a general graph $G$ by which family of inequalities (in addition to $x\ge 0$)?
choices: Degree constraints $\sum_{e\ni v} x_e \le 1$ only
Degree constraints together with odd-set inequalities $\sum_{e\subseteq S} x_e \le \lfloor|S|/2\rfloor$ for every odd $S$
Only the odd-set inequalities, dropping degree constraints
Spanning-tree constraints
questions.hint: Bipartite graphs need only degree constraints; the new content is the odd-set family for non-bipartite graphs.
questions.explain: Edmonds (1965): degree constraints alone are insufficient for non-bipartite graphs — the 5-cycle gives a fractional half-edge solution. Adding the odd-set inequalities for every odd $S \subseteq V$ exactly describes the matching polytope.

questions.q: Grötschel–Lovász–Schrijver (1981) established the equivalence:
choices: polynomial separation $\iff$ polynomial optimization (via the ellipsoid method)
polynomial separation $\iff$ polynomial enumeration of vertices
polynomial vertex count $\iff$ polynomial optimization
every integer program is polynomially solvable
questions.hint: The breakthrough was using the ellipsoid method with an oracle, not a list of constraints.
questions.explain: GLS: a polytope admits poly-time LP optimization iff it admits a poly-time separation oracle. The ellipsoid method only asks 'is $x\in P$? if not, give a violated inequality' at each iteration — so an oracle suffices, even if $P$ has exponentially many facets.

questions.q: The matching polytope of $C_5$ has a positive integrality gap. With only the degree constraints $\sum_{e\ni v} x_e \le 1$, $x\ge 0$, what is the fractional LP optimum of $\max\sum x_e$? (Recall: integer max matching of $C_5$ is $2$.)
choices: $5/2$ (attained by $x_e = 1/2$ on every edge)
questions.hint: On the cycle, the symmetric fractional matching sets every edge equal; check the degree constraints carry the load.
questions.explain: Setting $x_e=1/2$ on all 5 edges of $C_5$ satisfies the degree constraints with equality and gives objective $5/2$. The integer optimum is $\lfloor 5/2\rfloor = 2$, so the integrality gap is $5/4$. Adding the odd-set inequality $\sum_{e\subseteq V} x_e \le 2$ closes the gap.

questions.q: Threshold rounding for minimum vertex cover sets $\hat x_v = 1$ when $x_v \ge 1/2$, where $x$ is the LP optimum. What is the proven approximation ratio?
choices: Optimal — gives an exact vertex cover
2-approximation
$\ln n$-approximation
$O(\sqrt n)$-approximation
questions.hint: Every LP variable doubles at most when rounded, and feasibility is preserved on every edge.
questions.explain: For each edge $(u,v)$ with $x_u + x_v \ge 1$, at least one of $x_u, x_v \ge 1/2$, so the rounded cover is feasible. Cost at most doubles, giving a 2-approximation. This is also optimal under the Unique Games Conjecture.

questions.q: On a universe $U$ of size $n = 100$, the LP relaxation lower bound for set cover is $\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}$. The greedy algorithm produces a cover of size at most  $H_n \cdot \mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}$  where $H_n \approx \ln n + \gamma$. To two decimal places, what is $H_{100}$? (Take $\sum_{k=1}^{100} 1/k$.)
questions.hint: Use $H_n \approx \ln n + \gamma$ with Euler's constant $\gamma \approx 0.5772$.
questions.explain: $H_{100} = 1 + 1/2 + \cdots + 1/100 \approx \ln 100 + 0.5772 + 1/200 \approx 5.187$. So greedy / randomized rounding gives a $\approx 5.19$-approximation on this universe.

questions.q: What is the Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio for max-cut, and how is it achieved?
choices: $1/2$, by random partition
$0.878\ldots$, by SDP relaxation + random hyperplane rounding
Optimal (1), by LP
$3/4$, by greedy
questions.hint: The ratio comes from comparing $\theta/\pi$ to $(1-\cos\theta)/2$ over $\theta\in[0,\pi]$.
questions.explain: Goemans–Williamson (1995): solve the SDP $\max \sum_{ij\in E}(1-v_i\cdot v_j)/2$ with unit vectors $v_i \in S^{n-1}$, then round by a random hyperplane through the origin. The probability $(i,j)$ is cut is $\theta/\pi$, and $\min_{\theta} (\theta/\pi) / ((1-\cos\theta)/2) = \alpha_{\mathrm{GW}} \approx 0.878567$.
